topics.label: Lecture introduction and learning outcomes
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic frames the lecture by connecting it to the practicals and outlining its intended learning outcomes.

topics.label: Tumor virology and the discovery of cellular proto-oncogenes
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how studying tumor-causing viruses established that cancer can originate from altered normal cellular genes.

topics.label: Experimental tests of cellular transformation
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how experimental assays establish whether a gene or mutation gives cells transformed properties.

topics.label: Functional classification and effects of cancer mutations
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how cancer mutations are classified by their functional effects, using RB regulation and dominant-negative p53 to illustrate and qualify those classifications.

topics.label: DNA repair defects and genetic instability
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain sequence and chromosomal instability through the DNA damage that repair pathways normally correct and the consequences of defective repair.

topics.label: Genetic instability from replication and mitotic errors
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics show how failures in faithfully copying and distributing the genome during cell division generate instability that can promote tumor adaptation.

topics.label: Mutation timing in colorectal cancer progression
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic examines how the timing and order of mutation acquisition, particularly early genetic instability, influence colorectal tumor progression.

topics.label: Inherited cancer predisposition and the changing role of BRCA2 deficiency
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how inherited mutations accelerate cancer development, while the BRCA2 example qualifies this account by showing that the initiating deficiency need not persist for malignancy to continue.

topics.label: Lecture close and further reading
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic closes the lecture by inviting questions, recommending reading and announcing the next lecture.
